entities.summary:
Jean I of Alençon, known as the Wise, was a French nobleman and member of the House of Valois, born into a prominent Alençon family and educated at the University of Paris. He ascended to the throne of Alençon in 1404 following the death of his brother, Louis II, and married Alix of Armagnac. Jean I was a key figure in the Alençon-Charleville alliance, which played a significant role in the Hundred Years' War. He died at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, where he led a contingent of Alençon forces alongside the English and Burgundian armies against the French. Jean I's legacy extends beyond his military prowess, as he was known for his wisdom, diplomatic skills, and support of the arts and education. He was the first ruler of Alençon to issue a charter of liberties, recognizing the rights of his subjects and limiting the power of the nobility. His descendants continued to rule Alençon for centuries, shaping the region's history and culture.

Jean I's military campaigns were marked by victories at the Siege of Pont-à-Mousson and the Battle of Crécy, where he fought alongside English forces led by the Black Prince. His strategic alliances with the English and Burgundians helped to secure Alençon's position as a key player in the Hundred Years' War. Despite his military successes, Jean I's death at Agincourt marked the beginning of a period of decline for Alençon, as the region was eventually conquered by the French.

The legacy of Jean I of Alençon can be seen in the modern-day French region of Normandy, where the Duchy of Normandy was established in 911 and remained a powerful force in European politics for centuries. His support of the arts and education helped to establish Alençon as a cultural hub, with the city becoming a center for the production of illuminated manuscripts and tapestries. Jean I's commitment to the rights of his subjects and the limitation of nobility power also had a lasting impact on the development of constitutional law in France.
